sentences.text: This dinosaur was roughly two meters long and weighed about forty kilograms.
As an oviraptorosaur, it would have been covered in feathers but could not fly.
Its skull was deep, narrow, and short, featuring an arched crest.
The animal possessed three fingers, with the first being the largest and bearing a strong claw.
The genus Nemegtomaia was formally described by Lü and colleagues in 2005.
The type species, Nemegtomaia barsboldi, was originally named by the same team in 2004.
The first specimen was found in 1996.
Two additional specimens were discovered later in 2007.
Eggs found near the nesting specimen measured five to six centimeters wide and fourteen to sixteen centimeters long when whole.
Damage on the skeleton suggests skin beetles scavenged the remains.
The diet of oviraptorids remains uncertain, although their skulls resemble those of known or suspected herbivores.
In 2004, Lü and colleagues classified Nemegtomaia as an advanced oviraptorosaur most closely related to Citipati.
By 2010, Longrich and colleagues placed it in the family Oviraptoridae and subfamily Ingeniinae, noting it was the only member of that subfamily with a prominent crest.
Longrich and colleagues suggested that the crest might have evolved or disappeared multiple times among oviraptorids, or that Nemegtomaia may not belong to the subfamily Ingeniinae.
In 2012, Fanti and colleagues classified Nemegtomaia as a derived member of Ingeniinae closest to Heyuannia based on hand proportions.
Nemegtomaia lived in what is now Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous Period, approximately 72 to 70 million years ago.
Fossils are found in the Nemegt and Baruungoyot formations, which represent both humid and arid environments that coexisted.
Oviraptorosaurs, including Nemegtomaia, are known from Asia and North America and date to the Campanian-Maastrichtian ages of the Cretaceous period.
The family Oviraptoridae, to which Nemegtomaia belongs, consists of small members known exclusively from the Upper Cretaceous of Asia, particularly the Gobi Desert.
Gregory S. Paul suggested that crestless oviraptorids were juveniles or females of crested species, implying the number of genera in the group was exaggerated.
It is debated whether oviraptorids had temperature-dependent sex determination, as temperature differences in nests might have skewed sex ratios.
Research published in 2010 suggested that the jaws of oviraptorids, including Nemegtomaia, shared features with herbivorous animals.
A 2017 study proposed that the parrot-like jaws of oviraptorids might indicate a diet consisting of fruits, nuts, and seeds.
